content: Council Directive 67/548/EEC, adopted on June 27, 1967, serves as the primary European Union legislation governing the classification, packaging, and labeling of hazardous substances. This directive was established under Article 95 (formerly Article 100a) of the Treaty of Rome. It is also applicable in the European Economic Area (EEA) and aligns with relevant Swiss laws, ensuring compliance across these regions. Scope of the Directive The directive applies to pure chemicals and chemical mixtures (referred to as preparations) that are marketed within the European Union. However, it does not apply to substances created solely for research purposes. Additional rules for chemical preparations are outlined in Directive 1999/45/EC. The directive explicitly excludes the following categories of substances and preparations: Medicinal products Cosmetic products Waste materials Foodstuffs intended for human or animal consumption Pesticides Radioactive materials Furthermore, the directive does not regulate the transportation of hazardous substances or preparations. Classification of Dangerous Substances Article 2 of the directive categorizes substances and preparations considered hazardous. Some of these categories are associated with specific chemical hazard symbols and/or codes. The classifications include: Explosives (E) Oxidizing agents (O) Flammable substances or preparations, further classified as extremely flammable (F+) or highly flammable (F) Toxic substances or preparations, further classified as very toxic (T+) or toxic (T) Harmful substances or preparations (Xn) Corrosive substances or preparations (C) Irritants (Xi) Sensitizers Carcinogens (Carc), divided into three categories Mutagens (Mut), divided into three categories Substances or preparations toxic to reproduction (Repr), divided into three categories Substances or preparations hazardous to the environment (N) Substances or preparations falling into one or more of these categories are listed in Annex I of the directive, which is updated regularly. The European Chemicals Bureau maintains a public database of these substances. Danger Symbols The directive defines danger symbols in Annex II. A consolidated list of these symbols, along with translations into other EU languages, is provided in Directive 2001/59/EC. Standard Phrases Annexes III and IV of the directive define standard phrases that must be used in relation to hazardous substances and preparations. Annex III specifies phrases describing the nature of specific risks (commonly referred to as R-phrases), while Annex IV specifies phrases providing safety advice (commonly referred to as S-phrases). These standard phrases must appear on the product's packaging, label, and Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS). For substances listed in Annex I, the use of these phrases is mandatory. The most recent update to the lists of standard phrases occurred in 2001, and Directive 2001/59/EC provides a consolidated version in all EU languages. Packaging Requirements Article 22 of the directive outlines specific requirements for the packaging of hazardous substances and preparations. (Details are not provided in the text but are referenced for further expansion.) Labeling Requirements Articles 23 to 25 of the directive specify that the label on the packaging of a hazardous substance or preparation must include the following information: The name of the substance. For substances listed in Annex I, the name must match one of the names provided in the annex. If the substance is not listed, an internationally recognized name should be used. The name, full address, and telephone number of the entity responsible for placing the substance on the market (e.g., manufacturer, importer, or distributor). The appropriate danger symbols, if applicable. The relevant standard phrases, if applicable (with certain exemptions allowed). The EINECS number or an equivalent identifier. For substances listed in Annex I, the label must include the words EEC label. Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) Article 27 of the directive mandates that suppliers provide a Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) either in paper or electronic form at or before the first delivery of a hazardous substance or preparation. Suppliers are also required to inform users of any new, relevant information that becomes available. Directive 2001/58/EC offers detailed guidance on the preparation of MSDS documents. Transposition into National Law As an EU directive, this legislation is binding on member states but cannot be directly enforced against individuals or companies until it has been transposed into the national law of each member state. In the United Kingdom, the directive was transposed through The Chemicals (Hazard Information and Packaging for Supply) Regulations 2002 (SI 2002 No. 1689), commonly referred to as the CHIPS Regulations.
